text: 1 Lecture 1 1.1 Vector spaces Let F be a field. Informally, a field is a set of numbers equipped with the operations +, −, ×, ÷ that satisfy the usual arithmetic rules. A precise mathematical definition is not required in this course; for a rigorous treatment and an introduction to the beautiful Galois theory of fields, see [1, Chapters 13-14]. In this course, we will primarily focus on the cases where F = R, the field of real numbers, or F = C, the field of complex numbers. What is a vector? Mathematicians do not answer the question directly. Instead we answer the question what operations can be done on vectors. As long as these operations can be done, they are vectors. Definition 1.1. A set V is called a vector space (linear space) over F if it is equipped with addition V × V → V, (x, y) ↦→ x + y and scalar multiplication F × V → V, (a, x) ↦→ ax satisfying the following axioms: for any a, b ∈ F , x, y, z ∈ V (I) x + y = y + x, commutativity (II) (x + y) + z = x + (y + z), associativity (III) There exists 0 ∈ V such that x + 0 = x, additive identity (IV) For any x ∈ V , there exists −x ∈ V such that x + (−x) = 0, additive inverse (V) a(bx) = (ab)x, multiplicative associativity (VI) 1x = x, multiplicative identity (VII) a(x + y) = ax + ay, distributive property 1 (VIII) (a + b)x = ax + bx. distributive property 2 An element x ∈ V is called a vector and an element a ∈ F is called a scalar. Remark 1.2. The axioms above seems a lot, but they are just saying that the usual algebraic rules work for vector addition and scalar multiplication. This can be seen even more clearly in Proposition 1.3. It should be noted that the multiplication of two vectors is not defined within the structure of a vector space. Proposition 1.3. The following are direct consequences of the axioms (i) The element 0 ∈ V is unique. 1 (ii) For any x ∈ V , 0x = 0. (iii) For any a ∈ F , a0 = 0. (iv) If a ∈ F , x ∈ V such that ax = 0, then either a = 0 (in F ) or x = 0 (in V ). (v) For any x ∈ V , the element −x is unique. (vi) For any x ∈ V , (−1)x = −x. (vii) If x + z = y + z, then x = y. Proof. (i)-(vi) are left as exercise. We now proof (vii). We have x = x + 0 = x + (z + (−z)) = (x + z) + (−z) = (y + z) + (−z) = y + (z + (−z)) = y + 0 = y where we used (III), (IV), (II), the assumption, (II), (IV), (III) in each equality. Example 1.4. F n =         x1 x2 ... xn      : xi ∈ F, i = 1, . . . , n    equipped with addition      x1 x2 ... xn      +      y1 y2 ... yn      =      x1 + y1 x2 + y2 ... xn + yn      and scalar multiplication c      x1 x2 ... xn      =      cx1 cx2 ... cxn      . The zero vector is      0 0 ... 0      and the additive inverse of      x1 x2 ... xn      is      −x1 −x2 ... −xn     . Example 1.5. An m × n matrix A over F is an array of elements in F with m rows and n columns: A =      a11 a12 · · · a1n a21 a22 · · · a2n ... ... ... am1 am2 · · · amn      = (aij)1≤i≤m,1≤j≤n 2 where aij ∈ F for 1 ≤ i ≤ m, 1 ≤ j ≤ n. If the range of i, j are clear from context, we omit the range and write (aij). The set of all m × n matrices over F is denoted by Mm×n(F ). It is equipped with the addition (aij) + (bij) = (aij + bij) and scalar multiplication c(aij) = (caij). The zero vector is 0 = 0m×n an m × n matrix whose entries are all 0 and the additive inverse is−(aij) = (−aij). Then Mm×n(F ) is a vector space. As a vector space, Mm×n(F ) is simply F m×n, since a matrix can be flattened into a column vector with m × n components. Given a matrix A its transpose is the matrix At given by transforming its rows into columns. For example (1 2 3 4 5 6 )t =   1 4 2 5 3 6   . It is a convention in math to write a vector in F n as a column vector as we did in Example 1.4. But writing      x1 x2 ... xn      in the notes all the time takes a lot of space, so for the rest of the notes we make use of the transpose notation and write (x1, . . . , xn)t. Example 1.6. Let k ∈ N be a natural number and Ck(R) be the set of functions f : R → R whose derivatives up to order k are continuous. We also write C(R) = C0(R) for the set of continuous function. We equip Ck(R) with the usual addition (f + g)(x) = f (x) + g(x) and scalar multiplication (cf )(x) = cf (x) for c ∈ R. Then Ck(R) is a vector space over R. Example 1.7. The space Pn(F ) of polynomials of degree at most n consists of polyno- mials of the form p(x) = anx n + · · · + a1x + a0 where ai ∈ F for 0 ≤ i ≤ n. Under the addition (anxn + · · · + a1x + a0) + (bnxn + · · · + b1x + b0) = (an + bn)xn + · · · + (a1 + b1)x + (a0 + b0) and scalar multiplication c(anxn + · · · + a1x + a0) = canxn + · · · + ca1x + ca0 Pn(F ) is a vector space over F . 3 1.2 Subspaces Definition 1.8. A subset W ⊂ V of a vector space V is called a subspace if (i) 0 ∈ W (ii) For any x, y ∈ W , we have x + y ∈ W (iii) For any a ∈ F , x ∈ W , we have ax ∈ W Lemma 1.9. A subspace is a vector space. Proof. We first show that if x ∈ W then −x ∈ W . By Proposition 1.3 (v) and definition of a subspace, −x = (−1)x ∈ W . By the definition of a subspace, addition and scalar multiplication are well-defined on W . The axioms (I)-(VIII) are satisfied on W since they are satisfied for any vectors in V . Example 1.10. A line through the origin in R3 is given by {tv : t ∈ R} where v = (v1, v2, v3)t ̸= 0 is the direction of the line. A plane through the origin in R3 is given by {tv + sw : t, s ∈ R} where v, w are two vectors in R3 not parallel to each other. One can check that lines and planes are subspaces of R3. In fact {0}, lines, planes, R3 are the only subspaces of R3. Example 1.11. A matrix A is called a square matrix if the number of columns is the same as the number of rows i.e. A ∈ Mn×n(F ). A square matrix is symmetric if A = At. It is anti-symmetric if At = −A. The set of symmetric matrices and anti-symmetric matrices are subspaces of Mn×n(F ) can be seen as follows: 0 matrix is both symmetric and anti-symmetric and for any A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ) we have (A + B)t = At + Bt and (cA)t = cAt. Thus if A, B are symmetric, then (A + B)t = At + Bt = A + B and (cA)t = cAt = cA. The anti-symmetric case is similar. Example 1.12. Ck(R) is a subspace of Ck−1(R) for any k ∈ N. Pn(R) is a subspace of Ck(R) for any k ∈ N. Solutions to a linear differential equation form a subspace. Example 1.13. Let V = {f ∈ C2(R) : f ′′ + f = 0} with the addition and scalar multiplication from C2(R). Then V is a subspace of C2(R) since 0 ∈ V and if f, g ∈ V and c ∈ R, we have (f + g)′′ + f + g = 0 and (cf )′′ + cf = 0. In fact, we know from ODE that f (x) = c1 cos x + c2 sin x for c1, c2 ∈ R from which one can also check that V is a subspace. The point here is that we do not need the explicit formula for solutions to conclude that the set of all solutions form a subspace. 4 1.3 Span We want to build the vector space out of the smallest amount of vectors. Addition and scalar multiplication are the only operations we have in a vector space. If we have x, y ∈ V , then x + y and ax for a ∈ F can be built out of them. Given a set of vectors v1, . . . , vn what are all vectors that can be built from them? This is the idea of linear combination and span. Definition 1.14. Let V be a vector space over F . A linear combination of v1, . . . , vn ∈ V is a vector of the form a1v1 + · · · + anvn where a1, . . . , an ∈ F . The set of all linear combinations of v1, . . . , vn is denoted by span(v1, . . . , vn). We use the convention that span ∅ = {0}. Proposition 1.15. span(v1, . . . , vn) is a subspace of V . Proof. By Proposition 1.3 (ii), we have 0 = 0v1 + · · · + 0vn ∈ span(v1, . . . , vn). If x = a1v1 + · · · + anvn and y = b1v1 + · · · + bnvn are two linear combinations, then x + y = (a1 + b1)v1 + · · · + (an + bn)vn and cx = (ca1)v1 + · · · + (can)vn are both linear combinations of v1, . . . , vn. Thus span(v1, . . . , vn) is a subspace. Example 1.16. Let v1 = (1, 0, 0)t. Then span(v1) = {(a1, 0, 0)t : a1 ∈ R} is the line through the origin in the direction of v1. Let v2 = (0, 1, 0)t, then span(v1, v2) = {(a1, a2, 0)t : a1, a2 ∈ R} is the plane deter- mined by 0, v and v2. Let v3 = (1, 1, 0)t, then span(v1, v2, v3) = {(a1 + a3, a2 + a3, 0)t : a1, a2, a3 ∈ R}. This is the same as span(v1, v2) since it is just the set of points with x3 = 0. Let v4 = (0, 0, 1)t, then span(v1, v2, x) = {(a1, a2, a3)t : a1, a2, a3 ∈ R} = R3. Definition 1.17. v1, . . . , vn is a spanning set of V if span(v1, . . . , vn) = V . If V has a finite spanning set, then V is called a finite dimensional vector space. 1.4 Linear dependence and independence We see in Example 1.16 that v3 is redundant in building vectors i.e. adding v3 to v1, v2 does not change their span. We want to get rid of the redundant vectors to find the smallest set of vectors that span a vector space. The following concepts are important. Definition 1.18. v1, . . . , vn is linearly dependent if there exist a1, . . . , an ∈ F not all zero such that a1v1 + · · · + anvn = 0. v1, . . . , vn is linearly independent if or it is not linearly dependent, in other words, for any a1, . . . , an ∈ F such that a1v1 + · · · + anvn = 0 we have a1 = · · · = an = 0. Example 1.19. v1 = (1, 0, 0)t, v2 = (0, 1, 0)t are linearly independent since for any a1, a2 ∈ F we have 0 = a1v1 + a2v2 = (a1, a2, 0)t implies a1 = a2 = 0. 5 Example 1.20. v1 = (1, 0, 0)t, v2 = (0, 1, 0)t, v3 = (1, 1, 0)t are linearly dependent since v1 + v2 − v3 = 0. The previous examples shows that a linearly dependent set of vectors is not small enough i.e. it has vectors that is redundant and that linearly independent vectors are not redundant. Thus our goal of finding a smallest set of vectors that builds the whole vector space is to find a basis: Definition 1.21. v1, . . . , vn is a basis of V if span(v1, . . . , vn) = V and v1, . . . , vn are linearly independent.
